newsitem.title: GAMBIA: Tiny Gambia chooses new parliament on Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Tiny Gambia chooses new parliament on Thursday.

text.p: The tiny West African tourist haven of Gambia chooses a new parliament on Thursday in elections which effectively wrap up its transition from military rule.
The poll for 45 of parliament's 49 seats is widely expected to consolidate former military leader Yahya Jammeh's transition from coup maker to elected president.
Jammeh, who seized power in 1994 and was elected president last September, urged voters in a New Year message to turn out peacefully and in force for Thursday's election.

"The voter turnout for the (constitutional) referendum and the presidential election was, in each case, very good, but I invite you to make the one for the coming general elections the best ever," he said in a broadcast.
Jammeh, 31, toppled independence leader Sir Dawda Jawara accusing him of corruption.
His supporters are assured of six seats where no rival is standing against them. Jammeh nominates four legislators. Under Jawara, parliament had 36 elected and eight nominated members.

Jammeh banned established politicians before the presidential poll, denouncing their links with Jawara. Opposition in the nation has since gathered around lawyer Ousainou Darboe and his United Democratic Party.
Darboe, who is not standing for parliament himself, took refuge in Senegal's embassy for several days during and after the presidential poll saying he feared for his safety.
Campaigning this time has been peaceful.
Gambia, a poor, mainly Moslem ex-British colony of just over a million people, fronts the Atlantic Ocean and is surrounded by Senegal. Its economy is based on tourism, groundnuts and foreign aid.
Jammeh's coup estranged Western donors. Some advised nationals against visiting on security grounds, hitting tourism. Jammeh has since developed ties with Libya, Taiwan and Cuba.
Over 100 candidates are standing. More than 446,000 people are registered to vote. Polls open at 7 a.m. (0700 GMT) and close at 6 p.m. (1800 GMT). First results are expected Thursday.
